Gauḍapāda
------------------------------------------
In the Advaita Vedānta tradition, गौडपाद has been honoured as the teacher of Govindayogīndra who himself was the teacher of शङ्कर (A.

-820). He is said to have lived in the Badari-kāśrama in the हिमालयस् and acquired the knowledge of the उपनिषद्स् from Lord नारायण himself.
Whether the name ‘Gauḍapāda’ was his real name or only a cognomen indicating that he came originally from the Gauḍadeśa (Bengal?) is rather difficult to say. He might have lived around A.

.
There are seven works attributed to गौडपाद. They are:
The Kārikās on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad.
A bhāṣya (commentary) on the Sāṅkhyakārikā of ईश्वरकृष्ण.
A वृत्ति (concise commentary) on the Uttaragītā.
Śrīvidyāratnasūtra.
Subhagodaya.
A bhāṣya on the Nṛsiṁha Pūrva-tāpinī Upaniṣad.
A commentary on the Durgā-saptaśatī (same as the Devī-māhātmya or the Caṇḍī).
However, except the first, all the other works might be the compositions of a different गौडपाद.
The philosophy of गौडपाद, as reflected in the Māṇḍūkya Kārikā, is an extreme form of advaita. According to him, the avasthātraya-vivecana or an analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् reveals that all these states (jāgrat or waking, स्वप्न or dreaming and सुषुप्ति or deep sleep) are like night for the जीव or the individual सोउल्, since there is no direct and clear experience of oneself as the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् in these three states. It is only in the तुरीय (or the fourth) state that one’s आत्मन् nature is experienced. Hence, even the so-called ‘jāgrat or waking’ state is a state of sleep or इल्लुसिओन् or इग्नोरन्चे!
By giving the example of a fire brand, moved around fast, which creates optical illusions, गौडपाद tries to prove the illusory nature of this world.
‘Ajātivāda’ or the doctrine that this world is never created (ajāti = no birth) or born and that ब्रह्मन् alone is ever existent, is another theory that he puts forward with supporting लोगिच्. He vigorously refutes other theories like असत्कार्यवाद (the doctrine that effect never pre-existed in the cause) of the न्याय-Vaiśeṣika school, the सत्कार्यवाद (the doctrine that the effect did exist in its cause) of the Sāṅkhya philosophy as also the vijñānavāda (that विज्ञान or continuous waves of intellect alone exist) of the Buddhists. Ultimately he rejects his own अजातिवाद also since even the ajatva (non-birth) of the आत्मन् is kalpita or imagined!
However गौडपाद accepts praṇavo-pāsanā (meditation on the आत्मन् through प्रणव or oṁ) as the means for destroying द्वैत-ज्ञान or knowledge of duality.
Gauḍapāda also recommends asparśayoga or the योग of non-contact of the मिन्द् with any object, as an important mode of sādhanā. It is the same as ज्ञानयोग. In this practice, the मिन्द्, through the disciplines of विवेक (discrimination), वैराग्य (spirit of renunciation) and अभ्यास (repeated efforts) gradually gets dissolved—this state being called ‘amanībhāva’—since the objects of the world presented to the मिन्द् do not exist in reality. Hence, even as fire dies out when there is no fuel, the मिन्द् too stops working in the form of vṛttis or mental waves. The knowledge that the आत्मन् alone is real, becomes well-established.
Gauḍapāda concludes his Kārikās with a description of मोक्ष (liberation) and the mukta (liberated सोउल्). This description resembles the ones given in the Bhagavadgītā.
